raw_comment:
1.  The coastal areas are in danger of flooding, hurricanes and typhoons. Indeed, Akita Prefecture, Japan, which is the region where I live, is a coastal area, suffered  damage by flooding two years ago. Also, the equatorial regions are at high risk of heat stress and wildfires. 
2. I wonder why the risk of wildfires is higher in the parts of Africa, North America and South America, even  though they are coastal areas in a tropical climate. In most cases, the air in tropical  coastal areas  doesn’t really become dry, so the risk of  wildfires is low. 
3. According to the map, Japan, where I live,  is in danger of hurricanes and typhoons. Therefore, in my community, some buildings may fall down. In addition, there may be a power outage. 
4. Catchy headline : Prepare For a Natural Disaster!

raw_comment:
What do I notice: I notice that there is a lot of heat stress in areas near the equator, specifically countries in South America and Africa and an abundance of flooding risks near bodies of water.  I noticed that there are a lot of wildfires near areas that are affected by heat stress. Water stress is also located near the countries with heat stress.  Every country is impacted by some sort of climate crisis (dependent on both their geographical location and human population-e.g. how are resources being used, how are items being produced).
What I wonder:  I wonder what steps big corporations could take in the future.  A lot of the recent climate changes are being perpetuated by the bigger companies that use non-renewable resources. How they can grow to incorporate more environmentally friendly materials into their production processes?  Additionally, I wonder what else we can do from the perspective of a normal resident; how can we best advocate for measures to be taken against climate change and how we can carry out our actions sustainably.
What impact does this have on you and your community:  The impact it has on our community is catastrophic. Virginia would have an increased number of hurricanes and typhoons by 2040, and we wouldn't have the proper infrastructure.  Even prepping for these hurricanes and typhoons is not feasible in the near future, as the amount of resources to be used would be immense.

Headline: The Steady Climb to an Unstoppable Climate Catastrophe.

raw_comment:
Notice: I notice that every continent has Flooding and Water Stress. I also notice that the most water stress is predicted to be in Asia. The majority of heat stress is predicted to be in Mexico and Africa. I also notice that again the majority of Wildfires are predicted to be in Mexico and Africa. Is there a connection between these two factors?

Wonder: I wonder why many parts of Canada and Alaska are not affected by any of these risks. I wonder why Asia doesn't have much heat stress and additionally, why Asia doesn't have much heat stress but has lots of water stress. I wonder why just specifically the coasts of certain countries/ continents are predicted to have hurricanes and typhoons(i.e the east coast of USA and coasts of Australia and Asia) and why countries/continents are not impacted as a whole. 

Impact on Me and My Community: Virginia, where I live, is predicted to have lots of hurricanes and typhoons in 2040. This would impact me and my community by destroying homes, schools, and other landmarks that we call home. We as a community would loose many people and many people would loose everything that they had. The impact of climate change on my community specifically would be devastating and change all of our lives forever. 

What's Going on In this Map: 
"The Disastrous Consequences of Not Taking Action on Climate Change Now"

raw_comment:
Notice -
 I notice that no country is left unaffected by climate risks.
The sea level rising, hurricanes, and typhoons are of little risk when compared to the very large risks of heat stress, wildfires, flooding, and water stress, which are present in every continent (excluding Antarctica)
Wonder - 
Most likely areas will be affected by multiple risks, so how many other climate based risks are each of these areas facing?
Why there are large areas in northern Canada and Northeast Russia that are unaffected. 
Whether water stress is caused by drought or poor quality water
Impact on Community - 
My community like many others will be heavily impacted by climate change. This will change our everyday lives, making it even more important to educate ourselves and act now before this prediction becomes a reality.
What's Going on in This Graph - 
This graph shows the predicted risks caused by climate change by the year 2040
Headline- 
The devastation of climate change by 2040

raw_comment:
Noticed:  There is very little places on this map that are not affected by a climate risk.  I have noticed that since Northern Africa is really close to the equator, the main climate risk by that time will be heat stress.  The areas further from the equator like northern Europe will mainly struggle with flooding.  I have also noticed that most of the hurricanes/typhoons are in the eastern part of the world where even today it is common.  I have also noticed that the little bits of sea level rise is all near areas heavily impacted by water stress as well as flooding.

Wonder:  I wonder why hurricanes/typhoons, as well as sea level rise will not seem to be much of a climate risk.  I also wonder how in really cold places like Canada, how they will have wildfires.  

Impact:  This impacts my community because the effects of climate change will heavily reduce the quality of life.  Many of the every-day things we do, playing outside going for walks, playing in the snow, we most likely won't be able to do anymore.  It also effects future generations because they will be on the receiving end of the worst effects of climate change.  The only way to stop this is to put drastic limitations on greenhouse gases, force(not "encourage") companies to use only renewable energy.  We would have to change the government system completely to fix the looming threat of Climate Change.  

Title:  The threat of Climate Change, lets take a look into the future.

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Thematic world map** (categorical raster/choropleth-style map of global regions)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses a **single global map layout**.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Categories are shown by **color-coded geographic areas** across the map.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (global regions/land areas) | Spatial | Position on the map (x/y geographic position) |
| Top climate risk category | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of each mapped area |
| Flooding | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; blue color |
| Heat stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; orange color |
| Water stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; yellow color |
| Wildfires | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; pink/red color |
| Hurricanes and typhoons | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; teal color |
| Sea level rise | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; dark blue/purple color |
| Year 2040 | Temporal | Title text/annotation |

Notes:
- The map title indicates the subject: **“The Top Climate Risks Across the Globe by 2040.”**
- No numeric scale or axis is shown.

- One of the first things I noticed is the number of places that are affected by climate risks. There are very few places that are left unaffected by climate risks (like northern Canada, Greenland, and southern South America).
- Desert areas such as the Sahara face both heat and water stress.
- Forests like the Amazon Rainforest and the Congo Rainforest have a significant risk of wildfires.
- Only regions are affected by Hurricanes/Typhoons

Impact:
The area I live in is in the Eastern United States, which is greatly at risk of Hurricanes and Typhoons according to the map. In order to protect the people in this area who are at risk, we need infrastructure to avoid hurricanes.

raw_comment:
Notice: The first thing I notice is the location of each of the types of climate risks. The flooding risks are located near rivers, lakes, and the coast, wild fire risks, as well as heat stress, are located primary in the southern part of the world, and hurricanes/
typhoons are located along the coasts. Additionally, there are some countries at the top that don't have any climate risks, like Greenland, or most of Canada. 

Wonder: I wonder why none of the countries near the North pole have climate risks. Additionally, I want to know how this data was obtained. 

Impact: This has an enormous impact on me, my community, and the entire world. 2040 is not that far away and we have to cut our greenhouse emissions if we want a chance to save ourselves for this fate. These types of disasters cause the deaths of millions, the destruction of infrastructure, and harm to the Earth itself. 

Title: The World Needs to Cut Greenhouse-Gas Emissions or the Year 2040 is Going to be a Bumpy Ride.

1: What do you notice?
I notice how Africa will be filled with Wildfires, and notice how it'll also be surrounded with floods due to the melting of polar ice caps. I also notice how the top of Northern America will be filled with floods and the middle-bottom with hurricanes.

2: What do you wonder?

That's more than 10 average-sized neighborhoods combined. In conclusion, the risks that those tropical disasters will bring to us in our area will be tremendously harmful to our society.

raw_comment:
Notice: It doesn't look like there are any countries that have escaped the effects of climate risks by 2040. Coastal areas seem to have a higher risk of flooding, hurricanes, and water stress, while heat stress and wildfires are more prominent in central areas of countries. It seems there is the least amount of sea level rise. 

Wonder: I wonder why if flooding and other water related catastrophes are so prominent, sea level rise isn't? Why is there such a limited amount of sea level rise? Why are certain coast more prone to flooding, while others are more prone to heat stress?  What does heat stress and water stress mean? Why are areas, like Northern Canada, Greenland and parts of Russia, not subjected to any climate risks?

Impact: This will obviously have a huge worldwide impact. Just looking at the east coast of the United States, where I live, I see Flooding, Hurricanes, and typhoons on our top climate risks. This may be extremely catastrophic because our area isn't used to or prone to a lot of extreme weather.  And looking at the graph, it looks as though there won't be many places where these climate risks won't affect.

raw_comment:
Notice:
I've noticed that areas that would already experience these natural weather events would simply see the same things on a bigger level. For example, the eastern coasts of the United States and Asia have always seen hurricanes and typhoons, and areas of Africa and South America have always been incredibly hot. By continuing to emit greenhouse-gases at the frequency that we are, the effects of climate change will
exacerbate these already damaging conditions. This could put parts of the world that are already disadvantaged in worse condition. 

Wonder:
I wonder if any areas that usually experience one natural phenomenon could experience a different one due to climate change. 

Impact:
This impacts me because I live along the eastern United States and hurricanes could get much worse in my area. Bad storms could destroy my community, especially because there are lots of big trees that tend to fall on powerlines due to strong winds. Additionally, already disadvantaged parts of the world would struggle even more under the effects of climate change.

Headline:
The International Bully: Climate Change Kicks Communities While They're Down

raw_comment:
Notice:
I've noticed that areas that already see the weather events listed in the key will continue to see these events, just on a greater scale. The eastern coasts of the United States and Asia usually see many hurricanes and typhoons, similarly, areas of Africa and South American are no stranger to flooding. If we continued to emit greenhouse-gases at the frequency that we do, these naturally occurring weather events could become much more severe. 

Wonder:
I wonder if any areas that typically experience one type of weather event could experience another one due to climate change. 

Impact:
I live on the eastern coast of the United States, and we often are victims of the massive thunderstorms that can come with hurricanes. I live in an area with very big trees and lots powerlines, and during these storms, trees can fall on powerlines, cars, and houses. Stronger storms caused by climate change could result in more damage being done to my community, and endangering lives. However, I'm not the only person impacted by climate change. Areas of the world that are already disadvantaged could struggle even further, depending on the area and weather event.

raw_comment:
Notice: I noticed that every country faces a various number of risks when it comes to climate change. Several factors contribute to this, such as location, population, etc. For example, we can see that countries/locations that border bodies of water (seas and oceans) have the problem of flooding (i.e. parts of Canada). 

Wonder: 
- Why are there inland regions that are struggling with flooding (for example, Central Africa) - what is causing this?
- What is "water stress"?
- Does heat stress increase with population?
- If flooding is at risk, doesn't that directly imply that sea levels are rising (another risk)?

Impact: This data can impact me as it extends to 19 years in the future. This means that my family, friends, and I will still be alive during this time, and the fact that finding areas of land that aren't at risk is rare, it's concerning as our lives are at risk. 

Title: "19 Years of Redemption - How Climate Change Will Affect Your Future If We Don't Start Taking Action."

raw_comment:
1: What do you notice?
I notice how Africa will be filled with Wildfires, and notice how it'll also be surrounded with floods due to the melting of polar ice caps. I also notice how the top of Northern America will be filled with floods and the middle-bottom with hurricanes.

2: What do you wonder?
I wonder in what way, and how these disasters are going to affect Africa, and the whole world in general. Hurricanes in America are really going to destroy the economy, and the wellbeing of our country, and is going to take a pretty long time to rebuild/reconstruct.

3: What impact does this have on you and your community?
Based on the Key and map, I can tell that our area will be filled with floods, warm climates and worst of all, warm fronts. Greenhouse gases are also a big contributor to this issue. Using fossil fuels excessively is a big no-no, and is what's killing the ozone layer.  Aside from that, the hurricanes; a deadly type storm that kill hundreds, if not thousands of people per year. The Galveston Hurricane of 1900 killed an approximate of 8,000 people, or more. That's more than 10 average-sized neighborhoods combined. In conclusion, the risks that those tropical disasters will bring to us in our area will be tremendously harmful to our society.

raw_comment:
What do I notice?

Many places further north are experiencing more flooding. 
Most of northern Africa is experiencing heat stress
Central America is struggling with wildfires
The place where I live is experiencing hurricanes and typhoons.
Sea level is not being experienced in many places on the earth. There are very few blank white places on the earth

What do I wonder?

Why is Central America struggling with forest fires?
Why is Europe being flooded?
Why is the eastern part of the U.S experiencing Hurricanes?
Why is there no significant sea-level rise due to global warming?

Impact:

The area where I live is one of the only places on earth experiencing Hurricanes and Typhoons.

What Disaster is in Your Neighborhood?

raw_comment:
1.) What I noticed: I noticed that there is lots of flooding in countries with low altitudes near water. I also noticed that Greenland and Canada have the least amount of climate risks.

2.) What did I wonder: I wondered what other calamities other areas suffered. I wonder what the grey areas mean and do they have no risks? I wonder how these issues overlap and affect each other because this shows the highest risk but most places probably have multiple. I also wonder if it's possible to reverse this track we are on before 2040 without completely changing the global economy.

3.) What impact this has on me and my community: My community is heavily by Hurricanes and Typhoons and that could explain the many heavy rains and winds we got this summer. We don't typically get the brunt force of hurricanes, but we very much usually get the after-effects of hurricanes that hit the southeastern parts of the US.

4.) Headline: "Will YOUR area be habitable by 2040?"

Notice: I noticed that the flooding risks are along the coasts, or along the bases of mountains near the ocean. All of the hurricane risks are also along the coast but in more tropical locations so there's less of those spots. Wild fires and heat stress are in places already suffering from droughts or fires and tend to be in dry hot areas.

Impact: This graph impacts our community because we are in an area that is at risk of hurricanes and typhoons in the near future. This also puts us at risk of flooding, even though that's not explicitly stated, and other forms of damage.

Headline: The Risks of Not Changing 
Climate Change Projected Outcomes

raw_comment:
I notice that throughout places like Asia and the North, water stress and flooding will take over much of the land.  Heat stress also comes in big clumps, some examples being in Africa and South America. I also notice that sea level rise only comes in small dots affecting mainly the North. 
I wonder how much this graph will change over the next decade, and if there will be more or less white. I also wonder why there isn't as much heat stress in Asia as there is in Africa and South America, especially along the Equator. 
In my community, we will be impacted by minor flooding and hurricanes in 20 years, and a lot of the coastal cities may be in a bad state.

raw_comment:
I notice that throughout places like Asia and the North, water stress and flooding will take over much of the land.  Heat stress also comes in big clumps, some examples being in Africa and South America. I also notice that sea level rise only comes in small dots affecting mainly the North. 
I wonder how much this graph will change over the next decade, and if there will be more or less white. I also wonder why there isn't as much heat stress in Asia as there is in Africa and South America, especially along the Equator. 
In my community, we will be impacted by minor flooding and hurricanes in 20 years, and a lot of the coastal cities may be in a bad state.

raw_comment: I notice that many of the countries around the equator deal with heat stress and wildfires. Many of the countries near the North Pole are likely to have hurricanes and typhoons. Asia and Europe are the only continents with almost no wildfires or heat stress. I wonder why the middle of North America has the problem of water stress, when the other countries and continents have water stress near their borders. I also wonder why most of the islands deal with only flooding and not heat stress because most lay right on the equator. This has a huge impact on my community and me because this is the world that I'm going to live in for the rest of my life. Since I live in Virginia, the main climate risk is hurricanes and typhoons and those are devastating, like everything else. And if I move, there will always be climate problems in each area because there isn't one spot of land that is white on the graph. This map is showing the areas of climate problems around the world and how the problems depend on the location of the place. A catchy headline could be: "Wildfires, flooding, hurricanes, and more. What's happening where you live?"

## 1. Chart type
- **Thematic world map** (categorical raster/choropleth-style map of global regions)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses a **single global map layout**.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Categories are shown by **color-coded geographic areas** across the map.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (global regions/land areas) | Spatial | Position on the map (x/y geographic position) |
| Top climate risk category | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of each mapped area |
| Flooding | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; blue color |
| Heat stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; orange color |
| Water stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; yellow color |
| Wildfires | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; pink/red color |
| Hurricanes and typhoons | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; teal color |
| Sea level rise | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; dark blue/purple color |
| Year 2040 | Temporal | Title text/annotation |

Notes:
- The map title indicates the subject: **“The Top Climate Risks Across the Globe by 2040.”**
- No numeric scale or axis is shown.
raw_comment: I notice that many of the countries around the equator deal with heat stress and wildfires. Many of the countries near the North Pole are likely to have hurricanes and typhoons. Asia and Europe are the only continents with almost no wildfires or heat stress. I wonder why the middle of North America has the problem of water stress, when the other countries and continents have water stress near their borders. I also wonder why most of the islands deal with only flooding and not heat stress because most lay right on the equator. This has a huge impact on my community and me because this is the world that I'm going to live in for the rest of my life. Since I live in Virginia, the main climate risk is hurricanes and typhoons and those are devastating, like everything else. And if I move, there will always be climate problems in each area because there isn't one spot of land that is white on the graph. This map is showing the areas of climate problems around the world and how the problems depend on the location of the place. A catchy headline could be: "Wildfires, flooding, hurricanes, and more. What's happening where you live?"

raw_comment:
At first glance, the graph seems like a "who cares, right?" sort of graph, at least to me. I mean, this is set in 2040, and these are just predicted risks. (Unless scientists are hiding top-secret time machines." Besides. even if these risks do really occur, I can just move somewhere inland, preferably in a mountainous region. How does the Himalayas sound? I'll just go and build myself a literal man-cave, with all of those tchotchkes which are so necessary to survival.
But if we take a closer look, we see a trend that no matter where you are, either on the east (or is that west? Never eat soggy waffles- no, it's east. But west works too) coast or all the way in inland Russia, disasters are out to get you. It's not paranoia if it's real, right? Something I'd rather look at though is a comparison between the rate and severity of disasters now and disasters in the future, like a scatterplot with two populations. From the graph, we can't really tell what is increasing in severity and by how much. I mean, typhoons already happen on a regular basis near Japan. It's right up there with tsunamis and Godzilla attacks, and how much worse can it get? Besides, Kind Kong's gonna back us up.
Back on topic, however. I do believe that this graph is a good indicator of a trend: more disasters! Hoorah! But it could be made to be much more informative.

Title: Heat Waves, Wildfires and Godzillas: How Much More Will We Have to Take?

| Heat stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; orange color |
| Water stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; yellow color |
| Wildfires | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; pink/red color |
| Hurricanes and typhoons | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; teal color |
| Sea level rise | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; dark blue/purple color |

| Heat stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; orange color |
| Water stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; yellow color |
| Wildfires | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; pink/red color |
| Hurricanes and typhoons | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; teal color |
| Sea level rise | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; dark blue/purple color |
| Year 2040 | Temporal | Title text/annotation |

- No numeric scale or axis is shown.

raw_comment:
The real cost will be economic, as explained by a report issued by the central banking network ('Climate Scenarios for central banks and supervisors'). The potential economic cost is up to 35% of global GDP. As a similar report from the central bank network (BIS) states 

“Acknowledging the limitations of risk-based approaches
and integrating radical uncertainty suggests that, in the
age of climate-related risks, central banks may inevitably
be dragged into uncharted territory. .. Indeed, in the case
of economies that are no longer viable because of climate
change, central banks’ leeway could prove severely limited"

It is cost, not necessarily physical risk, which is the underlying feature. 

All these facts and a lot more (energy scenarios, fossil fuel exit etc) are explained in my book 'Planet Zero Carbon - A Policy Playbook for the Energy Transition', available on Amazon.

raw_comment:
I noticed that flooding, heat stress, water stress, and wildfires will be the most common climate risks throughout the globe. Almost every part of the world will be facing some kind of climate risk. The places that won't be facing a climate risk are mostly in the northern hemisphere. I wonder how the geography of each country affects its climate risk. I also wonder why some countries, such as South Africa have regions with no climate risk even though the rest of the country faces climate risks. Additionally, I wonder which human activities contribute the most to greenhouse gas emissions and their impact on each kind of climate risk. 

Where I live, in New England, the top climate risk is hurricanes and typhoons. Hurricanes can be devastating, especially in areas that aren't prepared for them. This graph can allow people to prepare for the climate risk greatest to their area. It also shows the importance of working towards reducing human impact on climate change. The idea of being threatened by so many natural disasters is scarier than the idea of changing our lifestyles to reduce our carbon footprint. 

A headline could be, "The Threats The World Faces if Carbon Emissions Are Not Reduced".

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I notice that wildfires, water stress, and heat stress are the most common climate risks to be faced.  It is clear that every continent will increasingly get hit by the listed climate risks. 

What do you wonder?

I wonder why people in developed countries try to pretend that climate change does not exist. While every country suffers from the disasters that are the outcome of environmental changes, developing countries have a much harder time: their financial stability can’t always be reliable, which makes rebuilding cities or towns after a disaster particularly difficult. Ignoring these problems will not make them go away.

What impact does this have on you and your community?

Climate change has forced many people to become climate migrants. They leave their lives behind because of the destruction to find better living conditions. Most of the time, these migrants go to developed countries such as the US, because of their financial stability. This means that the influx of migrants will rise with the increasing climate disasters in the coming years.
This impacts “welcoming cities,” who need to make new living arrangements and financial sacrifices.

What’s going on in this map? Write a catchy headline that captures the map’s main idea.

This map shows what countries and parts of the world will be affected by different climate disasters. 

Catchy headline: “We ignored it: Now it is coming full speed ahead.”

I notice that these issues are all worldwide, and each area has their own set of pollution induced problems. The whole world is affected by this pollution and therefore the whole world should act on it.

Everyone will be affected by this pollution, yet not enough people are talking about it or trying to adapt their lifestyle to save the earth.

## 1. Chart type
- **Thematic world map** (categorical raster/choropleth-style map of global regions)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses a **single global map layout**.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Categories are shown by **color-coded geographic areas** across the map.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (global regions/land areas) | Spatial | Position on the map (x/y geographic position) |
| Top climate risk category | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of each mapped area |
| Flooding | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; blue color |
| Heat stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; orange color |
| Water stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; yellow color |
| Wildfires | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; pink/red color |
| Hurricanes and typhoons | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; teal color |
| Sea level rise | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; dark blue/purple color |
| Year 2040 | Temporal | Title text/annotation |

Notes:
- The map title indicates the subject: **“The Top Climate Risks Across the Globe by 2040.”**
- No numeric scale or axis is shown.

- Not stacked.
- Categories are shown by **color-coded geographic areas** across the map.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (global regions/land areas) | Spatial | Position on the map (x/y geographic position) |
| Top climate risk category | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of each mapped area |
| Flooding | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; blue color |
| Heat stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; orange color |
| Water stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; yellow color |
| Wildfires | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; pink/red color |
| Hurricanes and typhoons | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; teal color |
| Sea level rise | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; dark blue/purple color |
| Year 2040 | Temporal | Title text/annotation |

Notes:
- The map title indicates the subject: **“The Top Climate Risks Across the Globe by 2040.”**
- No numeric scale or axis is shown.

I noticed that this graph depicts what climate risks certain continents have by the year 2040. These include flooding and water stress, heat stress and wildfires, hurricanes and typhoons, and sea-level rises. These risks don’t usually stick to one certain continent as they are normally scattered throughout the world.

This makes me wonder why the Arctic and Antarctica aren’t also having the same issue, but then again, it’s probably because they are the two coldest continents in the world, meaning that they have no problems with either of the risks. However,  it also made me wonder how the graph has this relatability to certain continents like since Australia had a forest fire before, it’s almost no surprise that it would expect more wildfires by 2040.

This impacts not only our country, but the whole world that needs to be prepared for any upcoming climate risks. Especially those that are at high risk of flooding and sea-level rise since floods are considered to be more lethal than the others.

I’ve decided to give this article the headline “If You Think The World Is Relatable Enough, Wait Till You See This” because looking at the graph, it slowly makes you realize how relatable this graph is because the people who live in those certain countries can relate to the struggle they have when it comes to climate change.

I noticed that wildfires were a big climate change factor in areas like California, Brazil, and Australia all of which saw devastating wildfires in the past two years. 
I wonder how and when there is going to be a big enough climate emergency for people to wake up and put the environment over monetary gain. Huge companies are responsible for the climate emergency and I really wonder will it be too late before something is done.

I live in Florida and have seen climate change first hand with a rapid increase in the amount of hurricanes we get per year. The Earth is telling us to stop destroying her and we have not heeded that call.

raw_comment:
What I noticed: The first thing I noticed was that based on what is most likely to happen based on climate risks helps you identify where you are even if you don’t know the geography of the land. For example, the big yellow and orange spot in Australia was a desert. I also noticed that flooding, water stress, and heat stress seem to be the biggest concerns with the potential climate risks.

What I wonder: I wonder what areas are at the highest risk because the graph only shows what the risk is. It would be good to see what areas are in the most need that way it is easier to prioritize what areas may need help. I also wonder how many areas are in danger of more than one climate risk. There are many areas that have two, three, or maybe more of these potential problems but I assume the graph just shows which one is most likely to happen. I also wonder what year these climate changes would be expected if greenhouse emissions were to increase or decrease. 

Impact: This graph has an impact on my community because we are at a high risk of hurricanes and also flooding. We have already experienced many hurricanes and they have been devastating to many families. Communities with this problem need to have a plan to provide support to those affected by floods or damage from storms.

Headline: Greenhouse Gas Emissions and the Potential Damage They May Cause.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that each continent has its own unique risks related to climate. For instance, North America has a lot of water stress and South America suffers from wildfires/heat stress. It is interesting to see how the top half of the map is dominated by hurricanes and typhoons but the bottom is not. Also, it appears that some risks have correlations, such as wildfires and heat stress. 
2. I wonder as to why the risk of wildfires is so common. Also, why does the top of the map differ from the bottom?
3. In terms of myself, this graph would be a great tool to use when choosing where to live. Sort of a pick your poison kinda thing. From a community standpoint, knowing the risks allows us to prepare/prevent them. Much the same to how people on the coast board their houses when a hurricane is coming.

all areas that produce food for other countries.

## 1. Chart type
- **Thematic world map** (categorical raster/choropleth-style map of global regions)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses a **single global map layout**.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Categories are shown by **color-coded geographic areas** across the map.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (global regions/land areas) | Spatial | Position on the map (x/y geographic position) |
| Top climate risk category | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of each mapped area |
| Flooding | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; blue color |
| Heat stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; orange color |
| Water stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; yellow color |
| Wildfires | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; pink/red color |
| Hurricanes and typhoons | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; teal color |
| Sea level rise | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; dark blue/purple color |
| Year 2040 | Temporal | Title text/annotation |

Notes:
- The map title indicates the subject: **“The Top Climate Risks Across the Globe by 2040.”**
- No numeric scale or axis is shown.
raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of this map:  "Climate Change's True Colors" by Kiernan and "Stop Greenhouse Gases Before It’s Too Late!" by Paige, both from Alaska, and “Impacts of Climate Change Will Be Devastating If Nothing Changes” by Julia and “A Map of the Apocalypse” by Paul, both of Memphis, Tennessee

 

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, April 2 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the map, and a few Stat Nuggets.

 

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).

View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 

graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 

Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex). 

 

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who has already experienced in Boston flooding, hurricanes, heat stress and sea level rises, and Heather Overstreet of Rocky Mount, Virginia, who is trying to reduce her carbon footprint.

- **Thematic world map** (categorical raster/choropleth-style map of global regions)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses a **single global map layout**.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Categories are shown by **color-coded geographic areas** across the map.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (global regions/land areas) | Spatial | Position on the map (x/y geographic position) |
| Top climate risk category | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of each mapped area |
| Flooding | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; blue color |
| Heat stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; orange color |
| Water stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; yellow color |
| Wildfires | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; pink/red color |
| Hurricanes and typhoons | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; teal color |
| Sea level rise | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; dark blue/purple color |
| Year 2040 | Temporal | Title text/annotation |

Notes:
- The map title indicates the subject: **“The Top Climate Risks Across the Globe by 2040.”**
- No numeric scale or axis is shown.

raw_comment:
In looking at this graph I notice all parts of the world besides the South and North Pole will be at climate risks around the world by 2040 if greenhouse-gas emissions are not cut drastically. I also notice that most of Europe and Asia will be effected by water stress and sea levels rising. I wonder why the Southern and Northern poles will not be effected really at all. This might be because of the fact there is little human life located in these areas which result in less greenhouse-gas emissions being released. This impacts my community because by the time of 2040, I will still be alive. If the world endures what this graph is showing, there will be serious damage to my country and world. I live in the Northeast of America which would be effected by hurricanes and typhoons. Hurricane Sandy and Irene destroyed New Jersey and caused us to go without power for weeks. If by 2040, we are hit with more hurricanes, who knows what the extensive damage will be. 
New Headline: "Climate Change is Real, Take a Look"

raw_comment:
I notice that there is a TON of concern for heat/fires all around the world. This is just a major concern because heat stress causes fires, and fires can cause habitat loss, life loss, just simply too much concern for fires all around the world. I also notice a lot of water stress. I assume this is concerning a lack of water, which is also a major concern, since it’s the most vital resource to any animal ever, including humans. I notice little to no sea level rises and hurricanes/typhoons. This is good and also bad. Hurricanes are one of the most devastating natural disasters ever, so this is just absolutely horrible for those affected, including myself.

I wonder what other disasters are in store for each region. This map shows the top climate risks, but that doesn’t mean some other risk is 0.01% less likely to happen there, which we need to keep in mind. I wonder if this will change in the future. It’s nearly impossible for us to cut down on greenhouse gases since we use these 24/7. Cars need them. Factories need them. It would be devastating to the economy, so I don’t think it would be possible at all. 

(1/2)

- **Thematic world map** (categorical raster/choropleth-style map of global regions)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses a **single global map layout**.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Categories are shown by **color-coded geographic areas** across the map.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (global regions/land areas) | Spatial | Position on the map (x/y geographic position) |
| Top climate risk category | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of each mapped area |
| Flooding | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; blue color |
| Heat stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; orange color |
| Water stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; yellow color |
| Wildfires | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; pink/red color |
| Hurricanes and typhoons | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; teal color |
| Sea level rise | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; dark blue/purple color |
| Year 2040 | Temporal | Title text/annotation |

Notes:
- The map title indicates the subject: **“The Top Climate Risks Across the Globe by 2040.”**
- No numeric scale or axis is shown.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that the country Greenland is almost empty. I also see that the US, China, and India are completely covered with different colors, meaning that these countries are at the worst risk for climate change. 
What do you wonder? 
I wonder if there’s a way to change what that map says. If we took extreme measures to fix climate change, how extreme would they have to be? Would those measures even work? Would other people even listen and follow guidelines to live more sustainably in order to slow down climate change? 
What impact does this have on you and your community?
I live on the coast of North Carolina, so the area I live in will most likely be affected by hurricanes and rising sea levels. I think that climate change will have a significant impact on the community I live in. Beaches and marshes are home to so many animals, and I’m sure that climate change will mess up the ecosystem they live in. 
What’s going on in this map? Write a catchy headline that captures the map’s main idea.
This map shows how climate change will worsen and continue to happen over the next few years. I think a catchy headline would be “The End is Near: Here’s the Effect Climate Change Will Have on the World in 20 Years.”

Climate change is a worldwide issue and many world leaders have met to address it. I wonder what are some actions private companies like Amazon, USPS, airplane companies, and transportation companies could take to help slow down greenhouse gas emissions within their own companies? If more horrific hurricanes and natural disasters were to occur it would be devastating to the communities who could potentially lose their houses, jobs, etc.

"Greenhouse-gas emissions and the threat it poses to the global world"

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s map shows the projected primary climate risks worldwide by 2040 if greenhouse-gas emissions are not drastically cut.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this map.

raw_comment:
What I notice: 
1. I notice that the places with the most wildfires and heat stress are South America, Africa and Australia.
 2. I notice that the places with the most flooding and water stress are Europe and Asia.
 3. I notice that pretty much every place has at least one climate risk except for Northern Canada, Russia and Greenland.
4. Compared to the other Climate risks, it seems like Sea level rise is the least common. 

What I wonder:
1. I wonder why Sea level rise is the least common Climate risk. 
2. I wonder if the higher the heat stress, the more the wildfires. 
3. I wonder if places above the equator line have more flooding because there is more ice that melts.

Impact on my community: 
In my community, the main problem is the wildfires and the trees in forests burn.  I think that the problems affect everyone, even if it is just mostly one problem. 

Catchy Title: What will your life look like in 2040?

raw_comment:
One of the first things I noticed was that there weren't a whole lot of locations that are not predicted to be impacted by climate change. It appears as though the most area is covered by either heat stress or water stress. It makes sense that most of the flooding is happening in the northern hemisphere because the ice and glaciers located there now will melt and cause flooding on the borders of Canada, Iceland, Greenland, Alaska, and Russia.  
One of the things I’m curious about is what's happening specifically on the coasts and the large bodies of water. Because we don’t see how the water is being impacted on this graph we also fail to notice the major changes happening in the habitats of aquatic animals, especially those in the northern and southern hemispheres. In my region specifically, we will suffer from heat stress and flooding which makes sense because it’s already starting to get warmer earlier in the spring and the temperature high’s in the summer also are getting warmer every year. Because of our  few moving bodies of water to remove excess water from our state, flooding is something that seems likely and happens pretty frequently in neighboring states in the summers. Both of these things combined makes me nervous for our economic health which is dependent on agriculture. When we suffer from high temperatures and flooding, it is going to be very difficult to continue to grow corn & soybeans at the same volume we are now. Where will you live in 2040? Choose Wisely!

## 1. Chart type
- **Thematic world map** (categorical raster/choropleth-style map of global regions)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses a **single global map layout**.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Categories are shown by **color-coded geographic areas** across the map.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (global regions/land areas) | Spatial | Position on the map (x/y geographic position) |
| Top climate risk category | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of each mapped area |
| Flooding | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; blue color |
| Heat stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; orange color |

| Year 2040 | Temporal | Title text/annotation |

raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed when examining this graph was the vast amount of water stress in the Middle Eastern region. This is concerning because competition for water can lead to pretty serious conflict. Not only is the Middle East predicted to suffer from severe water stress by 2040, but a large part of the United States as well.

Given these predictions, I wonder what is being done now to try and combat these issues on the horizon. What can we do now to possibly avoid these natural disasters from taking a toll on the world? I also wonder how these predictions were made and what data they collected to make these projections.

This information should greatly impact our community and the way we live our lives today because we want to lower the risk of these natural disasters wreaking havoc on our lives and the lives of the next generation. Cities, states, and countries around the world should make more of an active effort to decrease their greenhouse-gas emissions and be more environmentally friendly.  

Is It Worth The Risk?

raw_comment: I notice that this is a map about the primary climate risks around the world that would occur by 2040 if the globe does not drastically cut down greenhouse gas emissions. I can see that in the United States, the Midwest will face water stress, the West Coast will face wildfires and water stress, the Central areas will face stress and wildfires, and the Northeast will face hurricanes and typhoons. I also see that the color distribution matches horizontally across the globe, depending on the equator. I wonder as to why I have not heard of these potential things that could happen sooner, I am just finding about these problems may occur if we do not cut back on gas emissions. I also would like to know what the world is doing already, and if nothing, why are we not worrying about the future of the world. This impacts me and my community quite drastically because I live in the Northeast and I was pretty shocked to see hurricanes and typhoons in our area. When I think of those events, I picture them occurring in the South or in the tropics, never on the East Coast. As a result, I want to make sure that I am doing my part in staying green so that we can avoid these natural disasters as possible. raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
Water stress, flooding, and heat stress are the three top colors that cover the map. Water stress is particularly concentrated in the centers of land where they are not exposed to giant bodies of water, but instead there might be streams, rivers, lakes, etc. around those areas. Flooding is found largely at the borders of the land masses where they are exposed to large bodies of water. I also notice that heat stress is concentrated more around the equator. 

What do you wonder? 
I wonder that if there is supposed to be a lot of flooding, why are the sea levels not rising in the areas were there is supposed to be a lot of flooding? Will the flooding be caused by something other than rising sea levels? 

What impact does this have on you and your community? 
It seems that around Iowa, we’re most at risk for heat stress and flooding. I find this interesting, because most of the heat stress is around the equator, and in Iowa, we're not very close the equator. This will definitely have an effect on farming since Iowa is a very agriculturally centered state.

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
When looking at the map one of the first things I noticed was that heat stress was highest on the equator and close to the equator. Another thing I noticed was that floods mostly occurred on land close to the ocean with a few exceptions in Europe and Africa. Water stress for the most part also happens mostly in the Northern Hemisphere and on the bottom of South America, Africa, and Australia. 
What do I wonder?
One thing I wonder is what other effects would happen that aren’t shown on the map. There is nothing on Antarctica, but with greenhouse gas emissions it causes more and more of the ice to thaw. I wonder if this would be the cause for the sea levels to rise? I wonder how much the ice covered land will change in the next 20 years with the amount of thawing that would happen?
What impact does this have on you and your community?
I live in Iowa and looking at this map the biggest problem we would face is water stress. This is very bad considering that Iowa is an agriculture state. With a shortage of water our crops would not do as well and in turn it would cause us to have a shortage of food. We also have more farm animals than people and it could become a situation where we do not have enough water to give to the farm animals. 
Catchy Headline
“What the World Will Look Like in 2040 if WE DO NOTHING to Stop it”

4. This map predicts the main climate risks that the world will face by 2040 if greenhouse-gas emissions are not cut. A catch headline is "Cut the Gas".

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the majority climate risk that takes up most of the U.S is water stress. The majority for South america is heat stress. Overall there is a variety of climate risks for each country.
2. I wonder what contributes to each climate risk and what everyone in their country can do in order for it to die down.

raw_comment:
I notice that most of the water stress and flooding are above the equator while more heat stress and wildfires are south of the equator. I also notice there are very few areas that are predicted to be free from risks in 2040, those are areas that are less heavily populated areas.
I wonder if there are other risks that aren’t on the map because they wouldn’t be an issue globally but could be extremely detrimental to a certain area. I also wonder how interconnected these issues can be. For example, are some areas affected by more than one risk but one more so than the other so it's only labeled as "Flooding." Also, is the severity the same in all places that will be dealing with the same risk? Will the flooding be more severe in the Americas, Asia, Europe, or Africa, for example?
I can pick out that in my area, the risk will be between heat stress, flooding, and water stress. This is a prediction of the risks in the future that I will be a part of so I need to find action steps to reduce the risks of the problems specifically in my area.  
A title I would give this graph is RISK: The “Game” of  Our Future Disaster

## 1. Chart type
- **Thematic world map** (categorical raster/choropleth-style map of global regions)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses a **single global map layout**.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Categories are shown by **color-coded geographic areas** across the map.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (global regions/land areas) | Spatial | Position on the map (x/y geographic position) |
| Top climate risk category | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of each mapped area |
| Flooding | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; blue color |
| Heat stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; orange color |
| Water stress | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; yellow color |
| Wildfires | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; pink/red color |
| Hurricanes and typhoons | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; teal color |
| Sea level rise | Categorical/nominal category | Legend label; dark blue/purple color |
| Year 2040 | Temporal | Title text/annotation |

Notes:
- The map title indicates the subject: **“The Top Climate Risks Across the Globe by 2040.”**
- No numeric scale or axis is shown.

raw_comment:
I notice that this map provides us with a prediction of what dangers humanity will face in around 20 years if we do not see a drastic change in greenhouse gas emissions. I notice that the northernmost areas of the map have the least amount of climate risks (Canada, Greenland, and Eastern Russia are mainly unaffected). I also notice that sea level rising and hurricanes/typhoons are much less prominent on this map than I would imagine. Water stress, on the other hand, is much more prominent than I would expect.

I wonder how climate change affects water access. I also wonder when sea level rise is predicted to become a more prominent environmental problem. I wonder if flooding and sea level rising are connected issues. I wonder how exactly these climate risks could affect humanity and nature. Finally, I wonder how likely this future is. Is the world on a path towards changing our ways or is this future certain?

This impacts my community because Memphis as a city certainly contributes to greenhouse gas emissions. Memphis has many industrial zones which contribute to pollution, and Memphis is heavily sprawled, resulting in high emissions from vehicles. Finally, according to the map, our part of the world will face wildfires, heat stress, and flooding in the near future if greenhouse gas emissions are not cut.

| Year 2040 | Temporal | Title text/annotation |

- No numeric scale or axis is shown.
